bio.en: Vikrama Dhiman heads all product at Gojek - including product management, design, and research across India, Singapore, and Indonesia - and is one of Asia's best-known product leaders.
bio.zh: Vikrama Dhiman 统管 Gojek 的全部产品事务——包括产品管理、设计与研究，团队横跨印度、新加坡与印尼——也是亚洲最知名的产品领导者之一。

summary.en: Vikrama shares a practical framework for PM skill development, how to break into product management, and the common ways PMs shoot themselves in the foot. He discusses operating across diverse Asian markets, balancing breadth and depth as a product leader, and lessons from scaling Gojek's super-app. The episode is a grounded, mentorship-style guide especially useful for product managers in fast-growing markets.
summary.zh: Vikrama 分享了一套务实的“产品经理技能发展”框架、如何进入产品管理领域，以及产品经理常犯的自我挫败式错误。他讨论了横跨多元亚洲市场的运营、作为产品领导者如何平衡广度与深度，以及规模化 Gojek 超级应用中的经验。本期是一份扎根的、导师风格的指南，对快速增长市场中的产品经理尤其有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your name has come up more times than almost any other product person when I ask people for their favorite product leaders in Asia.

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: I created a career growth framework for product managers, which comprises of three things. What you produce, what you bring to the table, and what's your operating model.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your advice is early in your career, focus on just getting stuff out and done.
turns.zh: 在职业生涯早期，你的重点应该放在产出成果和完成任务上。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Can you show me your last PRD? Can you show me the last product note that you sent? Can you show me the product strategy doc? You must have that impact through the artifacts that you work on.
turns.zh: 能给我看看你最近的PRD（产品需求文档）吗？能让我看看你发送的最新产品说明吗？能让我看看产品战略文档吗？你必须通过这些实际成果来体现自己的影响力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious what you found most impedes people's career growth.
turns.zh: 我很好奇，您认为阻碍人们职业发展的主要因素是什么？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: How you view change, whether you are focusing on things you control, and third is how you see yourself. The moment you are able to correct those stories, you may be back on the growth path again.
turns.zh: 你如何看待变革？你是否专注于自己能控制的事情？第三点是，你如何看待自己？一旦你能够纠正这些认知偏差，你或许就能重回职业发展快车道。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Thank you for inviting me, Lenny. I'm very excited to be here.

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 正如你们所知，也希望听众们也知道，我正致力于结识全球最具洞察力的产品负责人。在向人们询问亚洲最受欢迎的产品负责人时，你的名字比其他任何产品人士都更频繁地被提及。而你也是 Gojek 的第三位嘉宾，看来那儿真是人才辈出，我很想探讨一下这个现象。直接切入正题吧，你在打造极具实力的产品人才和设计人才方面享有盛誉，还能帮助人们从其他岗位转型到产品管理领域——这正是许多听众梦寐以求的职业发展路径。因此，我将围绕这些领域提出一系列问题。听起来怎么样？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Sounds good.
turns.zh: 听起来不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. First question is just when you think back to the people that have done best in the product management role and have had a rapid career rise, what are some of the most common traits or behaviors or habits that you find in these people?
turns.zh: 好的。第一个问题是，当你回顾那些在产品管理岗位上表现出色、职业生涯发展迅速的人时，你发现他们身上最常见的特质、行为或习惯是什么？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Over the last decade and a half, I've had the opportunity to work with some really strong product managers, learn from strong product managers, and some of them have had rapid career growth. When I was younger and I was starting off, I used to think it's all about the product. If you've got a really cool product to work on, your growth's guaranteed. And if you got really a product which no one cares about or a stream which no one cares about, then your growth is going to be slightly slower. But as I started seeing more and more product managers at their craft, I saw that working on a cool product area is not the only thing. In fact, sometimes some product managers would come back and complain that despite their product doing really well, they've not really grown. (00:05:51): And while some other product managers whose product didn't have the impact really grew. And as I started looking at it and as I started making notes, as I started talking to other product leaders, what I discovered was that the really strong product managers who were also growing in their careers did some things differently. And based on that, I created a career growth framework for product managers, which comprises of three things, and I call it three W's. So what you produce, what you bring to the table, and what's your operating model? The really strong product managers are good at usually two of the three things. The ones who rise and when they are rising, they are performing well on all the three access. So if you would like, let's talk a little bit more about each one of these W's.
turns.zh: 过去的十几年里，我有机会与一些非常优秀的产品经理共事，从他们身上学习。其中一些人的职业发展确实非常迅速。当我年轻刚入行时，总以为产品是关键——只要有酷炫的产品可做，职业发展就水到渠成。而如果产品无人问津，职业发展就会慢很多。但随着我接触越来越多的产品经理，我发现产品领域并非唯一关键。事实上，有些产品经理会抱怨尽管产品表现出色，但自身发展却停滞不前；而另一些产品影响力不大的产品经理却能快速成长。在我深入观察、记录心得并与其他产品领导者交流后，我发现那些职业生涯蒸蒸日上的优秀产品经理在三个方面有所不同。基于此，我为产品经理们创建了一个职业发展框架，包含三个关键要素，简称为“三W”。即你产出什么、你能贡献什么，以及你的运营模式是什么？最优秀的产品经理通常能在三个方面中的两个方面表现出色。当他们晋升时，往往能在三个方面都表现优异。如果你愿意，我们可以详细探讨每个“W”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I would love to. I love that you put the word what at the top and that makes it the three W's, which is clever because I find even if the acronym is not necessary, it's really helpful to help people remember so I totally respect what you did there. So the three is what you produce, what you bring to the table and what your operating model is. Is that right?
turns.zh: 好的，我很乐意。我喜欢你把“what”放在开头，这样就成了“三W”，这很巧妙，因为即使不需要缩写，但能帮助人们记忆，所以我非常赞赏你的做法。那么三个方面分别是产出什么、能贡献什么，以及运营模式，对吗？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Yes, absolute.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Yeah, let's talk about these.
turns.zh: 好的，不错。让我们来详细讨论一下。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: So what you produce, a lot of people index on the impact while and they start thinking about goals, they start thinking about direction and they start thinking about strategy. While it is important to know at what stage of the career you are and what kind of a product that you are working on, the very first thing that anyone, when you're starting off, produces is outputs, okay? The output can be launching a product, it can be analyzing and running an experiment, and it could even be just being a part of the team and contributing to a go-to market strategy. So focus on that output significantly. As you get comfortable with output and you start getting comfortable with working with different stakeholders, you start controlling what outputs are necessary, which is when you move to the outcomes. Outcomes are product areas, goals that you can own and or collaborate with other stakeholders on. (00:08:14): And when you start figuring out which outcomes are necessary, that is when you move to the leadership and directional areas. The mistake that I see a lot of product managers make is they start operating in either output or outcomes. And when you are transitioning to outcomes, it's very important that you continue to still hone your craft on outputs. For instance, do you just give up on the go-to-market strategy or do you start making product nodes which are then picked up by marketing people and are able to be used to create that go-to-market strategy? You always, always have to have the output and outcome even when you're moving up the so-called career management ladder. So that is very, very critical that as you are producing, even when you are at the senior most levels, don't forget your IC roots, don't forget the IC component. And sometimes it is necessary to just pull up your sleeves and go back and keep working on those things. That also gives you a lot of creds with others in the team as well.
turns.zh: 正如你所说，很多人在职业生涯初期过于关注成果，却忽视了目标、方向和战略的制定。虽然了解自己所处的职业阶段以及手头项目的性质很重要，但对于初入职场的人来说，最初的任务就是产出成果——无论是推出产品、分析并执行实验，还是参与制定市场策略。应当高度重视这一产出阶段。当你逐渐适应产出模式，并与不同利益相关者合作时，才能开始思考哪些成果对团队最为重要，这时你就迈入了成果阶段。成果阶段意味着你需要明确负责的产品领域，或与其他团队协作达成共同目标。（00:08:14）而当你开始规划关键成果时，领导力和方向感便随之而来。许多产品经理常犯的错误是，要么只专注于产出，要么只关注成果。转向成果阶段时，务必保持产出能力的精进。例如，你是否会放弃制定市场策略，还是会构建产品节点以供营销团队借鉴？即便在职业生涯的顶端，产出与成果始终相辅相成。这就要求你即使身处高层，也要铭记工程师的初心，持续打磨专业技能。有时甚至需要亲力亲为，回归基础工作，这不仅能提升团队对你的认可度，更能为你赢得尊重。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So highlighting one insight here is that a lot of advice you hear about how to do well in your career, which you pointed out at the beginning here, is it's not just not immediately drive impact. That's not necessarily what you need to obsess over, which is actually what I recommend to people is just find ways to have impact. So this is really interesting. Your advice is early in your career, focus on just getting stuff out and done. Don't so obsess with the impact. Can you talk more about just what, when you say output, what are you describing there? Is it just ship products and be helpful and produce something?
turns.zh: 这里要强调的一点是，许多关于职业成功的建议（正如你开篇提到的），并非一味追求短期影响力。这并非你应过度执着的目标。相反，我建议初入职场者专注于产出成果，别急于追逐即时影响力。你的观点很有启发性：在职业生涯初期，要专注于完成任务，别过于执着于短期成果。能否请你详细解释一下你所说的产出阶段具体指什么？是简单地交付产品、提供帮助、创造价值吗？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Absolutely. So outputs is shipping products, but it also comes in smaller things. For instance, if you are sourcing content for your homepage, what are the different avenues that you can source content from? What is the easiest to source? What is the most difficult to source? Just ranking it all in that order goes a long way. And one of the product managers actually did that yesterday and I went, wow, it just made my life so much simpler. And not just my life but so many other people's lives so much simpler, and we were able to take that specific output and use it as part of our overall strategy. If that PM would have obsessed about the overall content strategy, overall how we are going to do it versus just how we are going to be sourcing it, they would have indexed on something bigger and maybe would have not even been able to make that impact. But now, they were able to show something which was a small part, which was an output, but it fell into the overall outcome.
turns.zh: 确实如此。输出当然包括产品交付，但它还体现在更细微的方面。比如，如果你需要为主页寻找内容素材，有哪些不同的渠道可以获取素材？哪些渠道最容易获取？哪些最难获取？把这些按优先级排列好会事半功倍。昨天就有位产品经理这么做了，我当时就感叹，哇，这真是让我工作轻松了许多。不仅是我的工作，很多人的工作都因此变得简单得多。我们能够将这项具体的输出成果纳入整体战略框架。如果那位产品经理一开始就纠结于整体内容策略，思考我们该如何规划整体策略而非如何获取内容素材，他们可能就错失了更宏观的视角，甚至可能无法产生这样的影响。但现在，他们能够展示出一个小成果——这只是一个输出环节，但它恰好融入了整体成果中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way I think about what you're describing, which I actually 100% agree with, is when you're starting out in your careers, execution is where you need to deliver. People just want you to get stuff done when you're just starting out. It's not like help us define our strategy and vision for the next three years. We just have stuff we need done. Can you help us get it done? Well, yes. And then essentially the advice is as you get more senior, you'll have more opportunity to think about strategy and what to build versus just how to build it and actually execute on it.
turns.zh: 我完全赞同你所描述的观点。在职业生涯初期，你需要专注于交付成果。刚入行时，人们只希望你能把事情做成。他们不会让你去定义未来三年的战略愿景，他们只需要你把眼前的事情做好。他们不会说：“帮我们制定战略愿景吧。” 而是会问：“你能帮我们把这事做好吗？”答案当然是肯定的。但随着职位晋升，你将有更多机会去思考战略方向、构建产品体系，而非仅仅专注于执行层面。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Absolutely. So focus on outputs at the start of your careers and don't forget outputs even when you grow in your career.
turns.zh: 确实如此。所以在职业生涯初期，要聚焦于交付成果，即便在职业发展中，也不要忘记输出的重要性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So along those lines, just to close the thread on this idea, it's still helpful if you work on something that does have impact that matters, right? How important is that? And you said that you've seen successful product managers work on things that aren't as impactful and still do really well, but I guess would your advice be tried [inaudible 00:11:52] be in a place that is going to drive more impact versus it's not actually that important in the early career?
turns.zh: 基于此，我想总结一下这个观点。只要你所做的工作能产生真正有价值的影响，那就依然值得深耕。这种影响有多重要呢？你提到过，有些成功的产品经理所做的工作影响力不大，但依然表现出色。但我想问的是，在职业生涯早期，是否应该优先选择那些能带来更大影响力的工作？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: So I'll give you my example. In one of my previous roles, there were two product areas that were important for the organization. My product area ended up being the center and focus of the organization, yet the product manager who was chosen to lead the area when it became big wasn't me. It was someone else. At that time, I really felt very bad that okay, why did that happen? But now when I look back, I can see why that happened because that product manager was so much better at the overall craft of output, yet when they were focusing on outcome, we're not forgetting the output as well. So they were just better at me on launching products, they were better at me on working with design, in producing design artwork, and they were definitely better than me in running the experiments as well.
turns.zh: 我举个例子。在我之前的职位中，有两个产品领域对公司至关重要。但当其中一个领域规模扩大后，被选中负责该领域的却不是我，而是其他人。当时我非常沮丧，心想为什么会这样？但现在回头看，我明白了原因——因为那位产品经理在输出层面的能力远超我，但当他专注于结果时，他同样重视输出环节。他在产品上线、与设计团队合作、制作设计素材，以及开展实验方面都比我出色得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Yeah, basically when you're just starting out, just execute well, execute smoothly, ship things on time. I'm going to say a few things, but I'm curious what else comes to mind here of just what does good output look like? Is it do things that are helpful to your team and manager, ship things on time, bug-free, have a clean road map, everyone's aligned behind, [inaudible 00:13:11] deadlines, things like that. I guess what else along those lines should people be like, "Okay, here's what I should be doing to have good outputs?"
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样。是的，基本上当你刚开始的时候，就要把事情做好，顺利完成任务，按时交付成果。我想说几点，但我很好奇还有什么其他想法——什么样的输出才算好？是做对团队和经理有帮助的事，按时交付无bug的成果，拥有清晰的路线图，让每个人都达成共识，[00:13:11的音频缺失]按时完成任务之类的。我想还有哪些类似的方面能让人觉得“好的，我应该怎么做才能有好的输出成果？”

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Some of the things that I think are useful. So first, what's output? Output is something which is very tangibly defined, which doesn't take too much of your time, effort, and energy to visualize and think and strategize over and you are able to quickly get moving on. Go and ask your product leader, go and ask other leaders on what are the areas they are blocked on. Sometimes they will be blocked on, "Hey, I need to prepare this brief for this particular summit", "I need to prepare this particular slide for a leadership review", "I need to prepare a review, I need to prepare a review which has to be done with the legal." You can volunteer and definitely own and deliver the first drafts of those even if the final draft is not something that you own. That's a simple example of an output, which I feel a lot of people miss because they want to be focusing on the bigger strategic pieces.
turns.zh: 我认为有一些有用的东西。首先，什么是输出？输出是可以非常明确界定的东西，不需要花费太多时间、精力和精力去构想、思考和策划，你就能迅速行动起来。去问问你的产品负责人，去问问其他领导，他们在哪些方面遇到了阻碍。有时他们会被阻碍在“嘿，我需要为这次特别峰会准备这个简报”，“我需要为领导层审查准备这个特定的幻灯片”，“我需要准备一份审查报告，我需要与法律部门一起完成这份审查”。你可以主动承担责任，甚至在最终版本不是你负责的情况下，也能完成初稿。这就是一个简单的输出例子，我觉得很多人都忽略了这一点，因为他们想专注于更宏大的战略层面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's basically be useful. That's the way I always like to talk about this, just like your job as a PM is be useful, make your team more effective, help your company be more successful. Just find ways to be useful to everyone around you.
turns.zh: 基本上就是要发挥作用。这就是我一直喜欢谈论这个问题的方式，就像产品经理的工作就是要发挥作用，让团队更高效，帮助公司更成功。只要想办法对身边每个人都有用就行了。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Absolutely. And be useful in doing the small things which make an impact and also contribute to your learning versus being useful in areas which you think the mini CEO should be working on.
turns.zh: 绝对的。而且要在做能产生影响的小事上发挥作用，也要为你的学习做出贡献，而不是在你认为微型CEO应该做的事情上发挥作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. There's all this talk about being an empowered product manager, building empowered product teams. I think there's an important nuance. When you're just starting out, you haven't earned the right to inform strategy and vision people. Why would people follow you at this point? We just need to get stuff done, so that comes over time.
turns.zh: 对。到处都在谈论成为一个赋权的产品经理，组建赋权的产品团队。我认为有一个重要的细微差别。当你刚开始的时候，你还没有资格去为战略和愿景提供信息。为什么人们会在这个时候听从你呢？我们只需要把事情做好，然后随着时间的推移，自然而然就会了。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Absolutely. And it's not just when you are starting off or when you are young. Even with if you are senior and you're starting off with a new team, even if you're starting with a new company, you need to have that mindset. And sometimes you will not know the best. And we'll talk more about how to, what is your operating model, which is how you work with others. It's a very, very important thing for you to know that you are one part of the cog wheel, you're not the entire wheel yourself. And a lot of the folklore around product managers can make you confused, especially when you're starting off in your career.
turns.zh: 绝对的。而且不只是刚开始或者年轻的时候。即使你是资深人士，刚加入新团队，甚至刚加入新公司，你也需要有这种心态。有时候你并不知道最好的做法。我们会更多地讨论你的运营模式，即你如何与他人合作。这对你来说非常非常重要，要知道你只是齿轮中的一环，而不是整个齿轮。很多关于产品经理的传说可能会让你感到困惑，尤其是当你刚开始职业生涯的时候。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Okay, let's keep going. Number two.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样。好的，我们继续。第二点。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Number two is what you bring to the table. Now, I think how I describe that is what is your impact on impact? So the first access is impact, but you also need to have an impact on impact. And this is what I had missed a lot in my early career, that you put the coolest product areas, your product area is successful and that automatically guarantees your growth. It doesn't. You have to also show that yes, you were a useful contributor to having that particular impact. The simplest thing on this is that is your PRD quality good enough? Are you writing that the draft notes that go and circulate to the care teams, to the marketing teams and so on? Are you making sure that you are deriving from the strategy that has been shaped or you're constantly just pushing back on the strategy? Similarly, you also how you are drafting the north stars, how you are working on the experiments, how you're working on the data, how you're working on the metrics. (00:16:43): All these things take time, effort, and energy. And I know there is some literature and there are some operating models where people are working only at strategy levels while all of these execution of these artifacts is being done by some other people. I don't think, especially when you are starting off, that's a very, very good thing. Even when you are mid-senior, I don't think that's a very, very good thing. You have to have to be able to produce these artifacts which are product artifacts. Even if there are people in strategy creating their artifacts, even if design is coming up with a design brief, you need to have a cohesive product strategy or product PRD and work backwards from PRD and product knows yourself. These things are important to show you are progressing on four pillars, which is data and metrics, design and research, technology skills, and strategy. (00:17:41): Product managers constantly are evaluated on this when you interview, but you also have to demonstrate these on the jobs. And the best way to demonstrate these is through the artifacts, through the notes that you are sending. So you must have that impact to impact through the artifacts that you work on. For a lot of product managers, when I ask, "Hey, I was working on this very impactful area. I'm not able to have the impact on my career, what is missing?" And when I go and ask, "Can you show me your last PRD? Can you show me the last product note that you sent? Can you show me the product strategy doc that you have or collaborated on? Can you show me the brief that you sent to the design team on the problems and the ranking of those problems?" Usually, you'll find something or the other missing. (00:18:31): In cases that those are bad, you will find that the pre-iteration planning, pre-sprint plannings are not running properly. You will find that the Jira storyboards are very empty and there's just a title in the subject and nothing gets described and so on. So you'll miss all these pieces. So these are the things which you bring to the table and it's very, very important that you work on these aspects as well. Finally, we have what's your operating model, which I feel is the most important thing which you have to have to focus if you are going from mid-senior to senior level. This is essentially about communication, collaboration, organizational skills and community skills. (00:19:16): And across product managers, again, because of the folklore of mini CEO and others, I see that a lot of people get carried away in the way they operate as product managers with other stakeholders. There are three tenets that I define in working well as a product manager with others. Number one is raise difficult issues without being difficult to work with. Bring out important topics without drawing importance to yourself. And finally, you are in charge of getting the decisions made and not making all the decisions yourself. I think as long as you follow these three tenets, you will have a successful relationship across stakeholders. These three tenets are easy to say, but they become very, very hard to embody and display on a day-to-day basis. But this is essentially going to be your struggle no matter at what level of product management you are operating at in your career or within your company.
turns.zh:
接下来要讲的是你能为团队带来什么价值。现在，我想用“影响力对影响力”来描述这个概念。首先，影响力本身很重要，但你还需要证明自己对影响力的贡献。这一点在我的职业生涯初期被严重忽视了——你可能会认为推出最酷的产品领域，产品成功了，就能自然保证你的职业发展。但事实并非如此。你必须证明自己确实为实现特定影响力做出了有益贡献。比如，你的产品PRD（产品路线图）质量是否足够高？你是否认真撰写了发送给产品团队、营销团队等的文档草案？你是否确保自己的工作源于既定战略，还是一味地挑战战略？同样，在制定北极星目标、开展实验、处理数据、优化指标等方面，所有这些都需要投入大量时间、精力和心血。（00:16:43）：我知道有些文献和运营模式主张产品经理只需专注于战略层面，而让其他人负责执行具体任务。但我认为，尤其是初入职场时，或者即使处于中高级阶段，这都不是明智之选。你必须能够亲自产出产品成果——即便有战略团队负责相关工作，比如设计团队制定设计方案，你也需要确保产品战略或PRD（产品路线图）连贯，并能从PRD倒推制定自身规划。这些能力的提升对于在四个核心维度（数据与指标、设计与研究、技术能力、战略）上取得进展至关重要。（00:17:41）：面试时，产品经理总会被评估这些能力，但实际工作中也必须能体现出来。最佳展示方式就是通过工作成果——比如发送的产品文档。因此，你必须通过实际产出证明自己能实现“影响力对影响力”的闭环。许多产品经理会说：“我曾参与极具影响力的项目，但未能转化为职业发展成果，问题出在哪里？”当我要求他们展示最新PRD、发送的产品文档、参与过的产品战略文档，或向设计团队提交的问题清单及优先级排序时，往往会发现存在缺失环节。（00:18:31）：在问题严重的情况下，预迭代规划、预冲刺规划执行不力，Jira故事板空洞无物，仅有标题却无具体内容等问题也会暴露。因此，这些能力的培养至关重要。最后，运营模式至关重要——这正是从中高级晋升至高级职位时必须关注的核心要素。它本质上关乎沟通、协作、组织能力和社区建设。（00:19:16）：受“迷你CEO”等刻板印象影响，许多产品经理在与其他利益相关者合作时容易陷入误区。我提出的三个核心原则是：

< 翻译说明：  
1. 术语如“PRD”（Product Roadmap）、“Jira storyboards”等保留英文缩写，必要时加注中文解释。  
2. 保持口语化表达，如“folklore of mini CEO”译为“迷你CEO的刻板印象”。  
3. 注意句子结构的流畅性，避免直译导致的生硬。  
4. 处理长句时，适当拆分或调整语序，确保中文表达自然。  
5. 最后通读译文，检查专业术语的一致性和整体连贯性。
定义如何与他人协作做好产品经理工作。首先，要敢于提出难题，但不让人觉得难以共事；其次，要能提出重要议题，但不刻意突出自己；最后，要负责推动决策达成，而不是独自包办所有决策。我认为，只要遵循这三条原则，就能与各利益相关方建立成功的合作关系。这三条原则说起来容易，但在日常工作中真正践行和体现却极具挑战。无论你处于职业生涯或公司内部的哪个产品管理层级，这注定将是你需要持续攻克的难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First of all, can you just repeat them? Because I think this is... Essentially, it's like a mantra that PMs can think back to of, "Am I doing these things?"
turns.zh: 首先，你能不能再重复一遍？因为我觉得这……本质上就像是一句产品经理可以回想起来的口头禅：“我是否在做这些事情？”

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: So the three things which are very important for product managers to work with others and other stakeholders are raise difficult issues without being difficult to work with, bring out important topics without drawing importance to yourself, and be able to get decisions made without having to make all the decisions yourself.
turns.zh: 所以，对于产品经理与他人及其他利益相关者合作而言，非常重要的三件事是：在不难合作的情况下提出难题；在不突出自己重要性的情况下提出重要议题；以及能够在无需自己做所有决策的情况下促成决策达成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like this list a lot. It reminds me, there's this product leader I worked with who their team got pushed to do a bunch of stupid stuff. And he realized later that, "Hey, it's actually my job to have pushed back on doing this stuff." He was the head of product for this business unit and he realized, "Oh, I see. That's actually what I should be doing now that I'm in this role." And you sometimes forget that one, you have that influence. And two, that's something you should be doing.
turns.zh: 我非常喜欢这份清单。这让我想起，我曾与一位产品负责人共事，他们的团队被迫做了很多愚蠢的事情。后来他意识到，"嘿，实际上我的职责本该是反对做这些事情的。"他是该业务部门的产品负责人，他意识到，"哦，我明白了。这才是我现在担任这个角色应该做的。"有时你会忘记这一点——你是有影响力的。其次，这也是你应该做的。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Absolutely, absolutely. It's always within your control and it's always the things that are within your control that you should be controlling rather than focusing on the things that are not within your control and obsessing about those.
turns.zh: 绝对，绝对。这始终在你的控制范围内，而你应该控制的正是那些在你控制范围内的因素，而不是关注那些不在你控制范围内的因素并为此焦虑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm so aligned with the way you think about all these things. Coming back to the second actually, just to give people something they can do with this trait. So the way I think about what you described, and correct me if I'm misinterpreting it, is there's a detail-oriented-ness, high quality-ness to the way that you should be crafting all the documents/artifacts you're creating, your one-pagers/PRDs, your roadmaps, your strategy docs, just like they should be really high quality. So along those lines, if you're an ICPM trying to get better at this stuff, how have you found is the best way to level up in these things? Is it working with your manager and getting feedback? Is it peers? What helps somebody get better at the quality and yeah, the quality of these documents?
turns.zh: 我非常认同你看待所有这些事情的方式。回到第二点，其实只是想给人们一些可以利用这个特质的方法。所以我对您所描述的内容的理解是，您应该以注重细节、高质量的方式来制作您创建的所有文档/工件——您的单页文档/产品需求文档、路线图、战略文档，应该都是高质量的。因此，如果您是一名ICPM，想要在这些方面有所提升，您发现的最佳方法是什么？是与您的经理沟通并获得反馈吗？还是与同行交流？什么能帮助某人提高这些文档的质量和质量？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: What you bring to the table is one of the most misunderstood attributes and aspects of product management. On one end, you could get around and say, "Here is my PRD, here is my JIRA board, here are my stories, here is my pre-sprint planning or pre-iteration planning document" and go. It's not just about the spread and the width of the things that you're doing, but it's also about the depth of those things as well. Some product managers, what they bring to the table is arguments, what they bring to the table are debates, what they bring to the table are pushbacks, while others are able to channelize the questions, channelize the inputs, channelize the direction and convert that into strategic choices which can then shape discussions, which can then shape direction. Be the latter and you will rise faster in your career.
turns.zh: 您所带来的东西是产品管理中最被误解的属性和方面之一。一方面，你可以四处转悠，说：“这是我的产品需求文档，这是我的JIRA看板，这是我的用户故事，这是我的预冲刺规划或预迭代规划文档”，然后就结束了。这不仅仅在于你所做事情的广度和宽度，还在于这些事情的深度。有一些产品经理，他们带来的只是争论、辩论和反击，而其他人则能够引导问题，引导输入，引导方向，并将其转化为战略选择，从而塑造讨论，塑造方向。成为后者，你的职业生涯会发展得更快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you have these three buckets of what you produce, what you bring to the table, and what your operating model is, the three W's. So let try to summarize and see what I missed and then we'll move on. So one is just focus on executing, getting things done that are helpful to your team, your company, your manager, and focus on just getting stuff out. Not so much in necessarily in strategy. Even when you're a manager and a leader and a VP, just like you're still responsible for producing things, not just telling people and being wise. Two, what you bring to the table, my takeaway here is produce high quality artifacts that raise the bar. (00:24:05): The way I think about this is as a PM, you want to have this aura of I got this. People put something on your plate, you want to feel like Lenny's got this, I'm not going to have to worry. It's going to be forgotten and I know it's going to be done well. And then the third piece is this idea of an operating model. Basically just make sure decisions are being made. It's not about you that you're pushing back on bad ideas. Is there anything else I missed before we move on?
turns.zh:
因此，关于你所产出的成果、你能为团队、公司和上级带来什么，以及你的运营模式（三个W），我们需要总结一下，看看是否有遗漏之处。首先，专注于执行，完成对团队、公司和上级有益的任务，重点在于产出成果，而非深陷战略泥潭。即使你是经理、领导或副总裁，你的职责依然是创造实实在在的价值，而非只是指挥和发号施令。

其次，“你能带来什么”——我的核心观点是，要产出能提升标准的高质量成果。（00:24:05）作为产品经理，你需要营造出“我能搞定”的气场。当别人把任务交给你时，你要让他们安心：即使忘了某些细节，你也能确保高质量完成。第三点是关于运营模式的构建，关键在于推动决策落地。关键不在于你是否反对糟糕的想法，而在于你的反对方式是否得当。切忌成为阻碍者和难相处的人，而是要被视为能为领导、利益相关方和产品领域的需求增值的人，推动产品向前发展。一旦做到这些，保持这种初衷，确保团队能突破障碍，不去做那些愚蠢或可能被改动的工作，你就真正掌握了要诀。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: No. I think the art of pushback is another important factor because if you're pushing back a lot and the way you are pushing back matters a lot as well. Just don't be someone who's seen as an obstacle and a hindrance and as someone who's just very difficult to work with, but rather see as someone who's able to actually add value to whatever your leader, your stakeholders, your product area demands and you are able to advance the product and the direction and execution forward. Once you do that, I think keeping that as the intent and ensuring that your team is getting unblocked and not getting to do work on anything which is stupid or is likely to be changed, then you've really got it.
turns.zh: 没问题。反驳的艺术是另一个关键因素。反驳过多固然不好，反驳方式也很重要。别成为被视为障碍、难相处的人，而要成为能为领导、利益相关方和产品需求增值的人，推动产品、方向和执行向前发展。一旦做到这些，保持这种初衷，确保团队能突破障碍，不去做那些愚蠢或可能被改动的工作，那么你就真正掌握了要诀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any advice for how to pushback in a way, the way you describe it is not to be difficult to work with or without seeking importance? I guess is there words or phrases or approaches you found are effective for pushing back against ideas that you disagree with?
turns.zh: 你对如何反驳有没有什么建议？你描述的反驳方式是既不难相处，又不寻求关注吗？我想有没有一些有效的词汇、短语或方法，能有效反驳你不同意的观点？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: What I've seen that people who do pushback very successfully and are still considered not difficult to work with, they are also able to bring the tempo of the conversation to a more logical space from an emotional space. I think that's such a useful skill and I sometimes am guilty of operating on a slightly emotional note, which is useful. Sometimes you need a war cry, you need a high pitch, you need execution on war footing. All that is fine, but it's only fine in some cases. In other cases, it's always very important that you're able to bring it down to the logical space so that a logical and a little more equal footing of the discussion can happen. And a lot of this is something that leaders need to ensure is happening, but product managers and product leaders who are working with executives who are able to bring this tempo down and bring it to a little more logical space will also do far better in their careers and they'll also have a lot more rapid career growth.
turns.zh: 我观察到那些反驳成功且仍被认为不难相处的人，还能将对话从情绪化层面引向逻辑层面。我认为这是一项非常有用的技能，有时我也会陷入略带情绪化的状态，这挺有用的。有时你需要振臂一呼，需要高声疾呼，需要以战时状态执行任务。这些都没问题，但只适用于某些情况。其他情况下，确保能将对话引向更理性的、更平等的层面至关重要。很多时候，领导者需要确保这种转变发生，但产品经理和与高管合作的产品负责人若能将对话节奏降下来，引向更理性的层面，他们的职业生涯也会更顺遂，晋升速度也会更快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's talk about the flip side of rapid career growth, which is career growth that stalls. And I'm curious what you've found most impedes people's career growth. What do PMs do that shoot themselves in the foot and slow their career? Any pitfalls do you find are important to try to watch out for?
turns.zh: 接下来让我们聊聊快速职业发展背后的另一面——即职业发展停滞不前的情况。我很好奇，究竟是什么因素最容易阻碍人们的职业成长？项目经理们会做哪些自毁前程、拖慢职业发展的行为？你们认为有哪些潜在陷阱值得格外留意？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: I think part of it is on a lot of us in product leadership space. We've not done a very good job in defining rubrics, growth frameworks and so on. But even in places where growth frameworks exist, like three W's, what I've seen is that clean mindset shifts and changes can enable faster growth, but those mindset and changes also can hinder your growth, right? So the first thing is whether you are focusing on things you control or whether you're focusing on things that are beyond your control. Second, what's your relationship with change? And third is how you see yourself. The third is very, very powerful and we'll talk about that as well. The first is what you control. If you drew an access of what you control and what you cannot control, as you're starting your career, most of the work that you're doing is in what you control, right? (00:28:15): You are very obsessed with feedback, you're very obsessed with, "Okay, can I do this?" "Can I do this?" "Okay, I'll probably not do this. I'll probably do this", and so on. You're not worrying about the overall corporate strategy, you're not looking at what the competitors are doing, what is their market cap and all those things. You're focused a lot on your craft, you're focused on a lot on your output and you're focused on how you are growing. As you start becoming mid-senior, I see the conversation shifts from what can I do, how am I learning, how am I growing, to why is the organization not doing this for me? Why can that stakeholder not change this thing about themselves? Why do I not get to work on projects like this? Things which start going outside your control. And it is very, very important that you keep your focus no matter what stage of career you get into what you can control. (00:29:16): And again, it's easy to say that everything in universe should be in your control. It doesn't happen like that, but a large number of things that impact your career are within your control. And go back to the three W's that we spoke about, what you work on, what you produce or what do you bring to the table, and what's your operating model? And there is tons to do on data, tons to do on technology, tons to do on communication, collaboration, design and research, strategy and community. And you can spend years and years and years crafting those things. Focus on those things, growth will happen at every single stage. The second aspect of it is your relationship with change. Again, when you are younger, when you're starting off, rate of change is crazy. You are growing almost every six months. You are picking up skills and experimentation, you're picking up skills in how to analyze. (00:30:15): You're picking up skills in how to work with different kind of stakeholders. And since the rate of change of your skills is high, your rate of growth is also high. Again, as you start becoming mid-senior, I start seeing conversations on, "Okay, maybe I should not do that. Maybe I should not take on this product. I don't know what it means for my career. I don't know what it means for my growth" and so on. So your rate of change slows down. So it's very important that as you get to mid-senior level, you are constantly checking on what you can do to keep increasing your rate of change. And one of the simplest things that you can do is if you think you are four on data, figure out who. And you may be four on data out of five in data. Within your organization, start benchmarking yourself with the best in the industry. (00:31:13): You'll automatically see that your scale drops and as your scale drops, you start seeing what you need to improve and do. If you start seeing that on communication and collaboration, you're reaching four out of five within the PMR, start mapping yourself to other stakeholders in other functions. Again, your score will fall in your eyes and you will start figuring out what are the things that you can do as well. So keep your focus on rate of change and rate of growth will automatically take care of itself. Sometimes it also involves changing your team or even changing your company, but those should be the last results. There are significant things that you can do within that as well. One of the final things that I see which limits you, especially as you start growing in your career and you reach mid-senior levels is how you see yourself. (00:32:04): I see a lot of product... And I've been guilty of that. When I see that a lot of product managers, that's included me at some stage, doing these things, people will come back and say, "Oh, I am a very high agency PM" or, "I'm a very collaborative PM." Earlier on, I used to think that okay, I need to give this kind of work to these product managers. I need to fit them with these kind of team, these kind of work areas, these kind of opportunities. But then I started understanding these things are not just signaling, they are also anti-signaling. They are like, "Oh, I'm high agency. So it's sometimes okay if I'm little brash, if I cut corners somewhere, if I sometimes come across as a little rude to some people" and so on, right? (00:32:55): Similarly, if I'm seen as a hyper-collaborative person, so it's okay if sometimes I'm not very decisive, if I'm not moving fast and so on because I'm this kind of a PM. So it's very important that you check for what are the stories that you're telling yourself because those stories are defining you at a basic level, which is then very hard to correct through frameworks and structures. So figure out what is the story that you are telling yourself. If you are not able to figure that out, talk to the people you trust so that they can tell you that as well, and then correct those stories. And the moment you are able to correct those stories, you may be back on the growth path again.
turns.zh:
我认为这在很大程度上取决于我们产品管理领域的许多人。我们在定义标准、增长框架等方面做得不够出色。但即使在存在增长框架的地方，比如“三W”模型，我发现清晰的心态转变和变革能够加速增长，但这些心态和变革也可能阻碍你的发展，对吧？所以首先要看你是在关注自己能控制的事物，还是超出控制范围的事物。其次，你与变革的关系如何？第三，你如何看待自己。这第三点非常重要，我们稍后会详细探讨。第一点是关于你能控制的事物。当你刚入行时，大部分工作都集中在你能控制的范畴内，对吧？（00:28:15）你非常执着于反馈，总是问“我能做这个吗？我能做这个吗？好的，我可能不会做这个，我可能会做这个”等等。你不操心整体的公司战略，也不关注竞争对手在做什么，他们的市值是多少之类的。你专注于自己的技艺，专注于产出成果，专注于个人成长。当你晋升为中高层时，我发现讨论话题从“我能做什么，我如何学习，我如何成长”转变为“为什么组织不为我做这些事？为什么那个利益相关者不能改变自己？为什么我不能参与这样的项目？”等等，这些问题开始超出你的控制范围。无论处于职业生涯的哪个阶段，都要始终专注于你能控制的事物，这一点至关重要。（00:29:16）当然，人们很容易认为宇宙中的一切都应该在你的控制范围内。但现实并非如此，不过影响你职业生涯的诸多因素确实在你的掌控之中。回到我们提到的三个W：你从事什么工作、创造什么成果、为团队带来什么价值，以及你的运营模式。数据、技术、沟通、协作、设计与研究、战略和社区等领域都有大量工作可做。你可以花费数年时间精心打磨这些领域。专注于这些方面，成长就会在每个阶段自然发生。第二个方面是与变革的关系。年轻时，起步阶段，变革速度快得惊人。你几乎每半年就成长一次，不断积累技能、进行实验，学习分析方法，学会与不同利益相关者合作。由于技能提升速度快，你的成长速度也很快。晋升为中高层后，我开始看到人们讨论：“好吧，也许我不该做那个产品。也许我不该接手这个项目。我不知道这对我的职业生涯意味着什么，对我的成长意味着什么。”等等。这时你的变革速度会放缓。因此，当你晋升为中高层时，持续审视自己如何提升变革速度至关重要。最简单的方法之一是，如果你认为自己在数据方面得了4分（满分5分），那就找出谁比你强。也许你在团队中数据能力只排第四。开始以行业内最优秀的人为标杆进行自我对标。（00:31:13）你会发现自己的水平在下降，随着水平下降，成长也会随之停滞。
看看你需要改进和做些什么。如果你开始意识到在沟通和协作方面存在不足，那么你在PMR中的得分应该能达到四分之三。接下来，你需要将自己与其他职能部门的利益相关者进行对标。同样，你的评分在你眼中会逐渐提高，你也会开始发现自己还能做些什么。因此，保持对变化速度和增长率的关注，自然就能达成目标。有时这甚至涉及调整团队或更换公司，但这些应该是最后的手段。在这方面，你也可以采取很多有效措施。最后，我发现限制你发展的因素，尤其是在职业生涯中晋升至中高层阶段时，往往在于你对自己的认知。（00:32:04）：我看到很多产品经理……我自己也曾犯过这样的错误。当我发现很多产品经理，包括我自己在某个阶段，都会做这些事情时，人们会回头说道："哦，我是一个非常注重客户关系的产品经理"，或者"我是一个非常善于协作的产品经理"。早期，我曾认为好吧，我需要把这类工作分配给这些产品经理，让他们适应这些团队、这些工作领域、这些机会。但后来我开始意识到，这些标签不仅是信号，也是反信号。比如，"哦，我很重视客户关系。所以如果我有点冒失、在某些地方偷工减料、对某些人有点无礼也无伤大雅"之类的，对吧？（00:32:55）同样，如果我被视为一个过度协作的人，那么如果我有时不够果断、行动不够迅速等，也是可以接受的，因为我就是这样的产品经理。因此，审视自己所讲述的故事非常重要，因为这些故事从根本上定义了你，而这很难通过框架和结构来纠正。所以，要弄清楚你给自己讲述的是怎样的故事。如果你无法做到这一点，就和信任的人聊聊，让他们也帮你指出问题，然后修正这些故事。一旦你能够修正这些故事，你可能就会重回增长之路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, there's so much meat and wisdom in what you just shared. I want to go in so many different directions. Maybe just to follow on this last thread, did you go through something like that yourself where you have this sense of yourself that hindered you? Okay, awesome. You're nodding your head, if you're not on YouTube. Can you share that?
turns.zh: 哇，你刚刚分享的内容真是太深刻、太有智慧了。我现在思绪万千，恨不得同时朝多个方向深入探讨。或许就从上一个话题延伸开来吧——你自己是否也曾经历过那种自我认知阻碍的阶段？好的，太棒了。如果你不在YouTube上，我看你正在点头呢。能分享一下吗？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Yeah. So I'll give an example of when I joined Gojek. The very first thing that I learned in my career was SQL and Oracle. And I was very proud of the fact that my data skills are awesome and I know several frameworks and I know several tools and so on. And when I joined Gojek and I saw one of your guests, Crystal, and I saw the work that she was doing and her team was doing and I just immediately was like, "Yeah, no, this is not... I'm nowhere near", right? And similarly, I also thought that my communication skills are really good and my product strategy skills are very good, but then I worked with people like Dito and people like Sidu who was so good at their craft that it challenged me to see that okay, what is it that I am missing? What is it that I am doing wrong? (00:34:57): And it auto-calibrated me in my eyes on where it was, but that also created a hunger in me that this is what I need to fix. And I immediately corrected my assessment of myself that I'm not the strongest product manager on data. I'm not the one who knows all the strategy pieces or even strategy frameworks or how to bring everything to a strategy point of view or communicate it from an effective perspective. And then I started framing I'm still in a learning phase. When I see that I'm not in that phase now, I try and make myself humble by interacting with people who are far smarter than me on different scale or reading different books, or watching podcasts like yourselves. And that keeps you grounded on the fact that okay, you are always learning. And I also found that seeing yourself as someone who's a learner is an enabling story to tell yourself, okay? (00:35:58): It may not be the most exciting story, it may not be the most memorable story about yourself, but it is definitely one of the enabling stories as well. Similarly, I think one other thing that I used to say about myself was more that I'm very high agency PM. But as I started working more in Southeast Asia, I learned that mindfulness is also very, very important, that not every team, not every culture will work with you in a very hyper aggressive style. But you still need to get the work done. And I'm still learning on that and therefore, I've started using a word, I don't want to be a high agency person, I want to be a mindful agency person. And so these terms are very important because these are the stories that you keep telling yourself and these also then start shaping your behavior. I do feel that I have a lot to do, I have a lot to learn on these skills, but these things definitely keep you grounded and you keep coming back to the learning phase again.
turns.zh: 是啊。我举个例子，刚加入Gojek时，我职业生涯学到的第一件事就是SQL和Oracle。我曾为自己的数据技能感到自豪，精通多个框架和工具等。但加入Gojek后，看到嘉宾Crystal及其团队的工作成果，我立刻意识到——“天啊，我差得太远了”。同样，我也曾自认为沟通和产品战略能力出色，但与Dito、Sidu等行业高手合作后，才发现自己的不足：策略框架不扎实，无法将数据与战略有效结合，缺乏有效的沟通技巧。这些反思让我重新审视自己，承认自己并非最强的数据产品经理。（00:34:57）这种自我校准让我意识到，永远在学习的路上。现在回看，我会保持谦逊——多与比我更优秀的人交流，阅读相关书籍，收听你们这样的播客，让自己始终保持学习的心态。将自己定位为学习者，也是一种自我赋能的故事。（00:35:58）这或许不是最激动人心、最令人难忘的个人故事，但确实是自我成长的基石。同样，我曾标榜自己是高强度行动派PM，但在东南亚工作后，我意识到耐心同样重要。并非每个团队、每种文化都适合高强度推进，但工作总要完成。我仍在学习，因此改口称自己为“有耐心的行动派PM”。这些定义至关重要，因为它们能塑造你的行为模式。我深知自己还有很多要学习的，但这些理念始终让我脚踏实地，回归到学习的初心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that when you saw Crystal being incredibly good at working with data, you just realized, "Hey, maybe I'm actually not very good at this." And your reaction wasn't, "God damn it, I'm really screwed and this is really depressing me", it's, "No, instead I'm going to try to get better at this." And that reminds me some of the feedback I get with this podcast, those people are like, "Man, these people are so good, I'm never going to be this good. It discourages me from thinking I will ever be super successful in this career." Clearly, you have a different approach. Do you have advice or guidance to folks that are sometimes discouraged seeing people being so incredible and helping them actually continue to level up in this rate of change you talked about versus just like, "Nope, I'm never going to be that good?"
turns.zh: 很有趣的是，当你看到Crystal在数据处理方面表现得极为出色时，你会突然意识到：“嘿，也许我在这方面其实做得并不好。”但你的反应并非“天啊，我真完蛋了，这真让我沮丧”，相反，你会说：“不，我要努力在这方面做得更好。” 这让我想起我在播客中收到的反馈，那些听众会说：“天哪，这些人太棒了，我永远也达不到他们的水平。这让我对在这一行取得巨大成功失去了信心。” 显然，你采取了不同的方法。对于那些有时会因看到他人如此出色而感到气馁的人，你有什么建议或指导吗？帮助他们在你提到的快速变化中继续提升自己，而不是简单地认为“不，我永远也达不到那种水平”。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: I think as product managers it becomes difficult because a lot of your growth is being determined because of feedback of others. And because product management is so ambiguous and still not defined, the stakeholders can also give feedback on variety of dimensions. Some of them may not even be important enough to give feedback on, but they are important enough for them and so therefore, they give you feedback. And therefore, you have to shape that feedback in. But you also have to consider that there are these eight access that we spoke about, the data access, the design and research access, the technology access, the strategy access, communication access, collaboration access, organizational skills access, and the community access. You need to channelize feedback into okay, is this an area that you are targeting for growth or not? (00:38:51): And one of the most important things that I learned was that when I joined Gojek or even earlier, there would be so many different areas that I needed to improve on and still need to improve on. You can't improve on every single area. That's what overwhelms you. You need to pick which is the area which is the maximum leverage for you and improve on that particular aspect and then move on to the next area, then move on to the next area and so on. Obviously, if you are floundering in something, if you're really negative in something, then you fix that first because that will give you the highest leverage. But if you are picking up data and design and strategy and technology all at the same time, that's when you'll overwhelm you.
turns.zh: 我认为，作为产品经理，这会变得很困难，因为你的成长在很大程度上取决于他人的反馈。由于产品管理是一个模糊且尚未被定义的领域，利益相关者可能会从多个维度提供反馈。其中一些反馈甚至可能不重要，但对他们来说却很重要，因此他们会给你反馈。你需要筛选这些反馈，判断这是否是你需要提升的领域。（00:38:51）：我学到的最重要的一点是，当我加入Gojek甚至更早的时候，我需要改进的领域太多了，而且至今仍在不断改进。你不可能每个领域都改进。这会让你不堪重负。你需要选择对你来说杠杆效应最大的领域，专注于提升那个方面，然后再转移到下一个领域，如此循环。显然，如果你在某个方面举步维艰，如果你对某件事态度消极，那么你应该先解决这个问题，因为这会给你带来最大的提升。但如果你同时尝试学习数据、设计、战略和技术，这时你就会不堪重负。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to summarize the advice there is one, be actually very open to feedback you're getting. It's easy to say that, it's hard to actually listen to people criticizing you and act on it. So I think that's an important takeaway here is just actually, feedback is a gift and actually understand that and try to act on it. I have a great interview with Jules Walter who's a PM at Google now, and he has this awesome quote about how whenever people give him hard feedback, it's like internally he's just melting, but that's externally he's like, "Thank you so much for that feedback, I really appreciate it. It's very valuable." (00:40:10): And so that's a good way to get people to keep giving feedback. Okay. And then the other piece of advice you just shared there is pick a focus area. Like say you're getting all this feedback, your strategy isn't amazing, your PRDs aren't great, just find one thing to focus on. And I don't know, do you try to do somewhat quarter? Somewhat year? Do you have a heuristic of how long to spend on one thing?
turns.zh: 总结一下这些建议，第一点是，要真正乐于接受反馈。说起来容易，但真正听取批评并采取行动却很难。所以我认为关键的一点是，要意识到反馈是一种馈赠，理解这一点并努力行动起来很重要。我采访了谷歌现在的产品经理朱尔斯·沃尔特，他有一句很棒的名言：每当有人给他严厉反馈时，他内心其实很受触动，但表面上却会说：“非常感谢你的反馈，我真的很感激。这对我很有价值。”（00:40:10）这就是让人们持续提供反馈的好方法。好的。接下来你提到的另一个建议是，选择一个专注领域。比如说，你收到了各种反馈，发现自己的策略不尽如人意，PRD（产品定义文档）也不够完善，那就专注于其中一项改进。我想知道，你是按季度还是按年来设定改进周期呢？对于某项技能的投入时长，你有没有什么经验法则？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: So different skills take different time and how you are progressing also depends a lot as well. For skills which are softer in nature like communication and collaboration and community, those are skills that you will work on all your life. You'll never achieve anywhere near two or five on five on those ever. There'll always be something that you will miss, there will always be a new context, there'll always be a new set of stakeholders, new company cultures that you have to adapt to. For others, you have to see that what gives you the maximum leverage in your career. When you're starting off, my recommendation is that you pick between data and tech one, and definitely one on design and research and strategy. (00:41:18): So usually, that's the combo that I recommend. My advice is if you're coming from design and research background, then you pick data or tech. If you're coming from a data or tech background, then you pick design and research, and that gives you the maximum leverage because that's a skill that you will necessarily not have developed over the years. Once you've demonstrated on two of these three, between data, tech and design and research, then you start focusing on strategy. We've had great success at Gojek in transitioning a lot of product managers, especially in Indonesia, using this framework. And it's produced a lot of good product managers for us.
turns.zh: 不同技能所需的时间不同，你的成长速度也因人而异。对于沟通、协作和社区建设等软技能，你需要终身修炼，永远无法达到五分满分的标准。总有遗漏之处，总有新环境需要适应，总有新的利益相关者和企业文化需要融入。对于其他技能，你要找到能为职业生涯带来最大杠杆效应的方向。初入行时，我建议从数据和技术中二选一，同时深耕设计、研究和战略。（00:41:18）通常我推荐这样的组合：如果有设计和研究背景，就选数据或技术；如果有数据或技术背景，就选设计和研究。这能最大限度地发挥你的优势，因为这些技能往往是多年未能精进的。当你在数据、技术和设计、研究这三项中掌握了两项后，再专注于战略。在 Gojek，我们成功地让许多产品经理转型，尤其是在印尼地区，效果显著。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let's actually follow that thread. That's really interesting. And so the approach is you have this access of skillsets and you pick, for this person moving from say customer service to product, here's the two things you need to focus on. Can you talk more about that?
turns.zh: 好的，让我们接着探讨这个思路。这真的很有趣。那么这种方法就是，基于技能组合来选择路径。比如说，对于从客服转向产品的人，要明确需要关注的两个方面。你能详细讲讲吗？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Yeah. For instance, we recently had two PMs, one who came from a growth background. This is actually [inaudible 00:42:24]'s team. And one from a research background. And with both of them, we use very different tactics. So we gave one of finding driver redesign, which was very much a very design-focused product, but we still had them leverage their data skills because we were able to create a PRD with incredible amount of data on exactly what different segments of customers we're doing. And that then we worked with designers on what the designs and the framework for that will be. And even now, Lenny, if you will come and see our finding driver redesign next time you are in Asia, it's a piece of art. And if you would see that that was worked on by a product manager who actually came from a growth and data background, that makes it even more special. (00:43:13): Similarly, the PM who transitioned from research, I kept giving feedback on technology and data skills are the ones that we need to check. And I need to hear from engineers that yes, they're able to work with her very strongly. And once she was able to do that, she's recently turned a very heated question on one of the features that we were doing into a full-blown solution with designs, with trade-offs and everything, and able to now convert it into a question for leadership on how we should be approaching this particular product and direction. So I think that's proven successful as well. Similarly, there's another person who took risk who was originally from research and again, worked a lot on our products, including our enterprise product. And she's doing an amazing job as well. Again, going through that path of okay, these are the things that you need to leverage. (00:44:14): The only watch-out is that it doesn't work out always. In some cases, some PMs will pick these things up fast, and it also makes a big difference if you are transitioning when you are slightly younger in your career. If you are already senior in a function and then you are transitioning, sometimes it can take a lot of time in transitioning and picking up those skills. But it's definitely doable if you get a very strong product leader working with you who's able to shape those skills for you. So it's sometimes okay to go a little slow when you're transitioning so that you're able to go faster later rather than getting faster somewhere and then being stuck there for a while.
turns.zh: 是的。比如说，我们最近有两位产品经理，一位来自增长团队，这实际上是[00:42:24无法听清]的团队。另一位来自研究团队。对这两位，我们采用了截然不同的策略。例如，我们让一位产品经理负责“Find Driver Re-Design”项目，这是一个高度以设计为导向的产品，但我们仍要求他充分发挥数据分析能力，因为我们需要用大量数据来精准描绘不同客户群体的行为模式。随后，我们与设计师合作，共同规划产品设计框架。即便现在，莱尼，如果你下次来亚洲时能参观我们的Find Driver Re-Design项目，那简直堪称艺术品。如果你得知这个项目是由一位来自增长与数据背景的产品经理主导的，那就更令人惊叹了。（00:43:13）同样，另一位从研究团队转型的产品经理，我不断反馈她需要提升技术和数据分析能力。我从工程师那里得到反馈，他们能与她紧密合作。一旦她掌握了这些技能，她最近就将我们正在开发的一项功能中的一个热点问题转化为一个完整的解决方案，包含设计方案、权衡利弊等内容，并成功将其提升为领导层需要考虑的战略方向问题。我认为这同样取得了成功。还有一位从研究团队转型的人员，她也参与了我们的产品工作，包括企业级产品，表现出色。同样，关键在于要明确你需要提升的技能。（00:44:14）唯一需要注意的是，并非所有转型都能顺利完成。在某些情况下，有些产品经理能快速掌握这些技能，但如果你转型时处于职业生涯中期，或者已在某个职能部门担任资深角色再转型，学习新技能可能需要更长时间。但只要有强大的产品负责人指导，转型是可行的。因此，转型初期放慢节奏也无妨，这样之后才能更快前进，而不是一开始速度过快却停滞不前。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: I think we've been in technology product for several decades now, but we are still figuring out what an exact definition of product management is. And even the strongest definitions are slightly principled and philosophical in nature, they're not very concrete, and that also means that every and different technology companies have gone through different journeys and they've defined the roles very, very differently. And even within a very large company, you will see that different teams, different divisions are approaching the roles very, very differently as well. (00:47:34): And on top of that, what that does is that not only internally the product managers are figuring this out, their managers, their leaders are figuring these things out for them, but the other stakeholders who have to work with these product managers are also confused and they don't know what to expect. And the number one question I get from stakeholders is, is a product manager expected to do this? Because they also don't know, okay, is this expected from a product manager or not? And my general answer to that is, if this is something which is blocking the progress on the product, then yes, the product manager should work on that.
turns.zh: 我认为，我们涉足科技产品领域已有数十年，但至今仍在探索产品管理的准确定义。即便最权威的定义也带有一定的原则性和哲学性，并非具体明确。这也意味着不同科技公司的发展路径各异，对角色的定义也大相径庭。即便在一家大型公司内部，不同团队和部门对角色的理解也千差万别。（00:47:34）：更糟糕的是，不仅产品经理自身在摸索定义，他们的上级和领导也在替他们思考定义，而与产品经理合作的其他利益相关者同样困惑，无法预知角色职责。利益相关者最常问我的问题是：产品经理需要做这些吗？因为他们也不清楚，这些职责究竟是产品经理的义务还是非义务。我通常回答：如果这些职责阻碍了产品进展，那么产品经理就应该解决它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: But that works if the product managers have had some training and they have had some training in working with different stakeholders and they have had something on the job. What I've figured out is that there are certain functions and there are certain disciplines which you can't define, but you can only become better at with practice. For instance, what is an actor or what is a dancer? Right? So these are things that you will get better at as you become skilled at it. And earlier, these things used to be looked at as something which is very artistic, only the people who are talented or only specific kind of people can do it. But now, each one of those has become [inaudible 00:48:57] and frameworks as well. So there are courses on filmmaking, there are courses on acting, there are courses on dancing and so on. And similarly, product management is that space as well. (00:49:08): So you have to understand there's an art to it and there's a science to it, but you can use the science to figure out the art. So that's the philosophical side of it. The second side of it is what we spoke about earlier that instead of figuring out what is product management, figure out what's your contribution, what's your output and figure out are you contributing on these access on data, on design, on technology and on strategy. And one of my favorite things is that if you created these four circles of strategy, of technology, of design and of data, and you created a product management circle which encircles each one of these, so you are the only discipline, which is the co-collaborator for all of these disciplines and tying all these things out. (00:49:59): So it's not about you standing alone, it's you always collaborating and pairing with someone else. But you are the only one who's pairing with everyone else and therefore, you have that unique insight which no one else in the team will have. That role can be played by someone else, it doesn't necessarily need to be called a product manager. But if you are being called a product manager, you figure out the [inaudible 00:50:24] the time piece that you are. And when you are added to the team, you must dream the team's overall contribution, overall energy and overall output up and not down.
turns.zh:
然而，这只有在产品经理接受过一定培训、善于与不同利益相关者合作，并且在工作中积累了经验的情况下才行得通。我发现，有些职能和专业领域无法被清晰定义，但只有通过实践才能不断提升。比如，演员和舞者是什么？对吧？这些技能是需要通过反复磨练才能精通的。过去，这些领域被视为极具艺术性的职业，只有天赋异禀或特定类型的人才能胜任。但如今，所有这些领域都已形成体系化框架——有电影制作课程、表演课程、舞蹈课程等等。产品管理领域同样如此。（00:49:08）所以你必须明白，产品管理既有艺术性，也有科学性，但你可以利用科学性来领悟艺术性。这就是其哲学层面的内涵。第二个层面是我们之前讨论过的：与其去定义产品管理到底是什么，不如先明确你的贡献是什么、你的产出是什么，以及你在数据、设计、技术和战略等方面的角色定位。我最欣赏的一点是，如果你将战略、技术、设计和数据这四个维度用圆圈围成一个产品管理圆圈，那么你就是连接所有这些学科的唯一纽带，是所有这些学科的协作者和整合者。
（00:49:59）所以这不是说你独自面对挑战，而是要始终与他人合作。但你是唯一一个与所有人合作的人，因此你拥有团队中其他人所没有的独特洞察力。这个角色可以由其他人来扮演，不一定非得叫产品经理。但如果你被称为产品经理，你就需要明确自己的角色定位。当你加入团队时，你必须为团队的整体贡献、整体活力和整体产出注入积极能量，而不是拖后腿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Something I always tell people is the PM doesn't necessarily have the magical skills other team members don't have, it's that they don't also have another job. Engineers may do a great job at being the PM, they just also have to build and code. And they don't have time to do all the things that a PM has to do, and a designer is in the same way, a researcher or data person. And so oftentimes, that's just like there's this person that has the time to do all these glue, work things between teams. And the great PMs also are very good at these skills that help you do these things, but it doesn't mean other people can't do them.
turns.zh: 我很赞同这一点。对此我常对人们说，产品经理不一定拥有其他团队成员所没有的神奇技能，而是因为他们不需要兼顾其他职责。工程师可能能出色地胜任产品经理的角色，但他们还要负责开发和编码，没有时间完成产品经理需要做的一切。设计师、研究员或数据分析师的情况也类似。因此，往往会有这样一种人，他们有时间在团队之间充当润滑剂，协调各方工作。优秀的产品经理也非常擅长帮助人们完成这些任务，但这并不意味着其他人做不到。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: You see yourself as playing a role and not your title and not your function, and that just clarifies a lot of things for people. And different people will play different roles. And depending on the kind of a PM you are, are you in a specific domain or you are slightly generalist, the role that you will be playing in different teams can be different and the variety of roles that you can play makes you a better product manager.
turns.zh: 你要把自己看作是扮演一个角色，而不是你的头衔或职能，这能让人们对很多事情有更清晰的认识。不同的人会扮演不同的角色。根据你所属的产品经理类型（是专注于特定领域，还是比较通才化），你在不同团队中扮演的角色也会不同，而你能扮演的多样化角色会让你成为更出色的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. You've mentioned these four access attributes of great product managers, overall product managers. Let's just spend a little time here. So you say basically the things you need to be doing and good at, data, design/research technology, strategy, and then you also mentioned collaboration and communication. Maybe you're-
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你提到的这些伟大产品经理和整体产品经理的四大核心能力特质。咱们就花点时间详细探讨一下。首先，你提到了产品经理需要具备和擅长的四项能力：数据、设计/研究、技术、战略，同时还提到了协作与沟通。或许你——

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Yeah, organizational skills and community. I think those are very, very important because one of the things and one of the things which one of the product managers works with me continues to say, and I really plus on that a lot, is that product manager is the all community enabler in the team, in the organization. And that community is the software aspect which ties everyone together towards a common mission of delivering an output. And that I think is a very, very important goal in today's context, especially for teams which are becoming more remote or teams where people are not co-located or they're distributed. That community aspect becomes a very, very important part that product managers need to focus on and bring and channelize as well.
turns.zh: 对的，组织能力和社区管理能力。我认为这些特质非常非常重要，因为与我共事的一位产品经理一直强调的一点，也是我深表认同的，那就是产品经理是团队乃至整个组织中连接各方的核心纽带。这个“社区”指的是软件层面的协作机制，它能将所有成员凝聚在一起，共同完成交付目标。在当今环境下，这一目标尤为重要，尤其是对于远程团队或分布式团队而言。社区管理能力已成为产品经理必须重点关注、培育和整合的核心能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's just quickly describe each of these attributes. I imagine people might be thinking, "Okay, what should I get better at as a PM?" And this is an awesome list. Each company has their own career ladders and attributes and things like that, but not a lot of companies don't. So I think for people that are trying to figure out where do I need to get better, I think this is a really cool list. Can you just maybe just a sentence explanation of each of these attributes and skillsets that a PM needs?
turns.zh: 接下来，我想快速解析每个能力特质。相信大家会想：“好的，我作为产品经理，应该在哪些方面提升？”这份清单堪称宝贵。尽管不同公司有各自的职业晋升路径和能力标准，但绝大多数公司都遵循类似框架。因此，对于那些正在探索自身成长方向的人来说，这份清单无疑极具价值。能否请您用一句话简要说明每个能力特质以及产品经理需要具备的技能？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: So each one of those skills, like the most growth ladders, what they will do, is they will have say for data, they will have level one, exhibits these traits. Level two, exhibits this trait. Level three, exhibits this trait. Level four and level five and so on. That's how they'll describe it. But five is absolute ninja level data quality, like you could probably do a data startup of your own.
turns.zh: 每个能力特质都设有成长阶梯。例如，数据能力的初级阶段表现为具备初步数据分析能力，中级阶段展现出更强的数据洞察力，高级阶段则能胜任复杂的数据建模任务。最高级别（五级）则需达到数据领域的专家级别，足以独立创办数据分析初创公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like Crystal basically?
turns.zh: 比如Crystal框架？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Crystal. And level zero is someone who cannot even basically define the basic metrics for this particular product and won't be able to figure out is this particular thing impacting orders or users or revenue. And so you'll really not be able to figure even that piece out. Similarly, on design and research, for product managers, we focus a lot more on problems and are you able to identify problems from a user's perspective. That's at level zero. And level five will be somebody who's able to define the user problems but is also able to tie them to business roles as well. So that makes it the holistic. Similarly, on technology, it's one of the skills which is relatively easier to define where you don't have any tech understanding. If somebody asked you what is HTTP or API or internet and you'll be like, "Okay, I don't know what it is." (00:54:55): And while on the other end, you are able to have deep debates and could probably write technology design documents yourself as well. I think sometimes people get confused between data science. And in different organizations, I see data science bucketed either in data or in technology. Either is fine as long as you are clear on what your organization's framework is. Similarly then, there is strategy. Strategy is I think another area in product management which gets very confusing because there is obviously corporate strategy, there is business strategy, there's pricing strategy, there's strategy everywhere. Product strategy for me is where you are able to define that while somebody defines that this is the mountain that you're going to climb, but okay, how are you going to climb that mountain is basically the product strategy piece. (00:55:47): So you are not in charge of okay, are you focused on growth? Are you focused on revenue? Are you focused on profitability? That's someone's choice. Are you going to pick this country? Are you going to pick that country? But once that is picked, what are the user segments that you're going to focus on? What are the needs of those user segments? How are we going to figure out what the right product for them will be? What is the order in which we are going to work on that? That whole piece of product strategy is with the product managers. And again, in the first case, you are basically going to rely on everyone to tell you, do this, do this, do this. In second and in the level five cases, you are able to articulate a very coherent product strategy at a broad level as well.
turns.zh: 克里斯托。零级别的人甚至无法基本定义这款产品的核心指标，也无法判断某个特定因素是否会影响订单、用户或收入。因此，他们根本无法理清这些问题。同样，在设计和研究方面，产品经理更关注用户视角下的问题识别。这就是零级别。五级别的人不仅能识别用户问题，还能将其与商业角色相结合。这才称得上是全面的。在技术方面，技术知识相对容易界定——如果你被问到HTTP、API或互联网是什么，你可能会说“好吧，我不知道”。（00:54:55）而另一方面，你也能进行深入的技术讨论，甚至可能自己撰写技术设计文档。我认为有时人们会将数据科学与其他领域混淆。在不同组织中，数据科学被归入数据或技术部门。只要你的组织框架清晰，这两种归类方式都可以接受。同样，战略也是产品管理中容易混淆的领域，因为显然存在企业战略、商业战略、定价战略等各种战略。但对我来说，产品战略是指当有人定义“这座山必须攀登”时，你要思考如何攀登。这就是产品战略的核心。（00:55:47）所以，你不必负责“专注增长？专注收入？专注盈利？”这些都是别人的选择。你不必选择这个国家或那个国家。但一旦选定后，你要关注哪些用户群体？他们的需求是什么？如何为他们设计合适的产品？按什么顺序推进？这些都是产品经理需要负责的。在第一种情况下，你基本上只能依赖他人告诉你该做什么；在第二种和五级别情况下，你能够在宏观层面清晰地阐述产品战略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing, thanks for sharing that. I think for people that are trying to craft career ladder for product managers, this could help inform the way they think about this. By the way, when we mentioned Crystal, for folks that have no idea who we're talking about, she was a early head of growth at Gojek back in the day. She was a previous guest on the podcast. I always forget how to pronounce her last name exactly, but I think it's Widjaja, Crystal Widjaja.
turns.zh: 太棒了，感谢分享这些内容。我认为对于那些试图为产品经理规划职业晋升路径的人来说，这可以帮助他们调整思路。顺便说一下，提到Crystal时，对于不了解她的人，她曾是Gojek早期的增长部门负责人。她之前也是我们播客的嘉宾。我总是记不清她的姓氏怎么拼，但我想是Widjaja，Crystal Widjaja。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Widjaja.
turns.zh: Widjaja。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Widjaja? Okay, okay. Great. Going in a different direction, we're going to move to contrarian corner. I'm curious if there's anything that you believe that other people wouldn't agree with or generally just don't believe?
turns.zh: Widjaja？好的，好的。接下来转到“逆向思维角”环节。我很好奇是否有你认为其他人不会认同，或者普遍不相信的观点？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: I used to think intent is the most important thing, right? And when I was starting off, that used to be the advice that as long as your intent is right, even if some of your words are not landing, even if some of the comms are not landing, that will work out. What I've seen is that it's not enough. Your actions, your behavior, and the way you communicate, the way you collaborate, that also has to communicate and show who you are as well. So intent is not enough. And that's a thing which I think a lot of people in my age group just don't get, but people who are slightly starting off their career, it resonates well with them. Second thing I think where I feel that it's become, I don't know, is it contrarian or it's become politically incorrect, is that you still need to put in the effort and our number of hours is effort. (00:58:23): And I think that's one thing which has become very politically incorrect to say over the years when I was younger, it was the norm that yes, you will have to put in the effort, you will have to put in the hours to grow and improve your skills. And it's not even about your growth in the company, it's just your own growth. You have to spend the time, effort, and energy into growing. I think a lot of that is getting lost in the debates between complete workaholism and just being not very serious about your growth at all. So I think those are the two that I find myself having to explain myself again and again and why I feel this way.
turns.zh:
我曾经以为，意图是最重要的，对吧？刚开始创业时，有人告诉我，只要你的初衷是正确的，即使有些话没说到点上，甚至有些沟通不畅，也能成功。但我发现这远远不够。你的行动、行为方式，以及沟通协作的能力，都必须能传达并展现出你的真实面貌。所以仅有意图是不够的。我觉得这一点在我们这个年龄段的人中常被忽视，但对于刚踏入职场的人来说，却深有共鸣。  

接下来我想说的是，意图不足已成共识，但有些人仍难以理解。比如，你依然需要投入时间和精力——时间本身就是努力的证明。（00:58:23）：在我年轻时，人们普遍认同“必须付出努力、投入时间才能成长和提升技能”，但如今这已被视为政治不正确。问题在于，人们忽视了成长的本质——不只是在公司里晋升，更重要的是自我提升。必须投入时间、精力和能量来实现成长。  

在“彻底的工作狂”和“对成长不重视”这两种极端观点之间，人们迷失了方向。这两点是我反复需要解释的，也是我坚持这种观点的核心原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I completely agree with that. I find a hugely strong correlation between hours you put into the work you do and success. And I think there's been a return to okay, working hard is really important and you shouldn't be afraid of promoting working really hard. So we've actually gone through everything that I wanted to ask you. Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, is there anything else you wanted to share or is there anything you want to leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 我完全同意你的观点。我发现投入工作的时间与成功之间存在着极强的关联。如今人们重新认识到，努力工作确实重要，不必羞于提倡这种精神。我们的对话已接近尾声。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？或者有什么想留给听众的建议？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: No, I think it has been great talking to. I hope it was useful to people. I've tried to keep it real, but also in takeaway format. And if there are any questions that you have that I feel I have not answered, I'm happy to answer them.
turns.zh: 没有了。和大家交流很愉快，希望对大家有所启发。我努力保持真实且易于理解的分享风格。如果还有未解答的问题，我很乐意解答。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, amazing. Well, we'll have people post in the comments if there's anything else they would love to ask you. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，请推荐两到三本你最常向他人推荐的书籍？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: The first book is a book which I feel is not quoted enough in product management community, is a book called Small Data by Martin Lindstrom. This is a person who was an advertiser or marketeer who would go and make campaigns for big brands in different countries, and so would have usually very short time to get the pulse of that space and design a campaign around it. And how he got insights very quickly from, and what are some of the takeaways that are there for people working in product space, not just product managers, but designers, researchers, strategy people, anyone really, I can't recommend that book more. And I've cited that book a lot internally. (01:01:09): The second book that I recommend is Adam Grant's Originals. I think it's a very important book. It changed a lot of things. When I spoke about that I was going through this crisis of, oh, I'm behind so many things after joining Gojek, Originals was one book that I read which really, really helped me think about my growth and how I see myself. And anyone who is stuck or anyone who feels they are superstars, they are the innovators of the century kind of a thing, it's a book that gives you a very good reality check. And the third book that I recommend is definitely Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow. I think especially the thinking slow part becomes very, very important piece as well. (01:02:11): And the reason why change is hard, the reason why feedback is hard is because we are used to thinking fast and we are not used to thinking slow. While if you actually think slow, you'll actually welcome change and growth.
turns.zh:
首部书籍是马丁·林德斯特伦（Martin Lindstrom）的《小数据》（Small Data）。在我看来，它在产品管理领域被引用得不够多。这位曾为各国大品牌策划营销活动的广告人或营销人员，通常只有极短的时间去了解市场动态并围绕其设计营销方案。他如何能迅速获取洞察，以及对产品领域从业者（不只是产品经理，还有设计师、研究员、战略规划师等）的启示，我再怎么推荐这本书都不为过。我在公司内部也多次引用过它。（01:01:09）  

我推荐的第二本书是亚当·格兰特（Adam Grant）的《创客》（Originals）。我认为这是一本非常重要的著作，它改变了许多人的观念。当我谈到这本书时，正经历着加入 Gojek 后进度落后的困境，《创客》让我重新审视自己的成长，重新定义自我定位。对于那些陷入瓶颈，或自视为天才创新者的人，这本书能给出深刻的现实考量。  

第三本必读之作无疑是丹尼尔·卡尼曼（Daniel Kahneman）的《思考，快与慢》（Thinking, Fast and Slow）。尤其书中关于“慢思考”的部分，同样至关重要。（01:02:11）  

变革之所以艰难，反馈之所以困难，是因为我们习惯了快速思考，却不善于慢思考。而当你真正放慢思考节奏时，才能欣然迎接变化与成长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That book's come up a bunch actually recently on the podcast and it is always sitting under my laptop, holding up my laptop for these interviews. So I fully agree. Next question, do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?

I thought it's a very fun movie, but also had a pretty good message. I know it's probably not the movie which anyone would want to cited, but I think it's sometimes good to just watch good entertainment.
turns.zh: 最近没怎么看电影。不过从迪拜飞回来的航班上，我又看了一遍《选美女皇》（Miss Congeniality），非常过瘾。这部电影很有趣，传递的信息也很棒。我知道它可能不是大家常引用的佳作，但有时看看轻松娱乐的内容也不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's quite the contrarian pick. Yeah, nobody has cited this movie, Miss Congeniality. This is a first, but I love it. It's way out there. I would never would've expected this.
turns.zh: 真是个反常的选择。是啊，没人提到过《选美女皇》。这是第一次，但我喜欢它。太出乎意料了。

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman

I think it's a show which operates at so many different levels without taking itself that seriously, and it just lands. And especially as a product manager and as a leader who obsesses a lot about diversity, I think it did a fantastic job in showing different sides of motherhood, of the LGBTQIA communities, and also teenage girls figuring themselves out as well. I think it did a fantastic job.
turns.zh: 说到电视剧，我常回看的是《富家穷路》（Schitt's Creek）。这部剧在多个层面都处理得非常自然，又不失幽默。特别是作为产品经理和关注多样性的领导者，我认为它在展现母性不同面貌、LGBTQIA群体，以及少女自我探索方面做得极为出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates when you're hiring product managers especially?
turns.zh: 您在招聘产品经理时，尤其喜欢问哪些面试问题？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: So it's not really one question, but what I like to do with them is to brainstorm choices on an actual product. And I'll typically pick up a product that they use most often and then I will be like, "Okay, what if this product were to do this? Then what do you think, it makes sense? Don't think it makes sense? What about this? Okay, how would it evolve in six months? What would happen in 12 months and so on?" I think it gives you a far better insight into how would it be on working with them on a real case. And you also keep... And what I like about it is that you can keep going back deeper into it and develop it together. So I typically try and pick product that I will also not have very strong opinions on so that it can become a two-way conversation.
turns.zh: 实际上这不是一个具体的问题，但我喜欢和他们一起针对实际产品进行头脑风暴。我通常会拿起他们最常使用的产品，然后问：“好，如果这个产品能做到这一点呢？你们觉得可行吗？觉得不可行呢？再看看六个月后会如何发展，12个月后又会怎样？”我认为这能让你更好地了解如何在实际案例中与他们合作。同时，还能不断深入探讨，共同完善方案。因此，我通常会选择自己意见不那么明确的产品，这样就能形成双向交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you actually look for in an answer that tells you, "Okay, this candidate is amazing" versus flags that are like, "Hmm, maybe not?"
turns.zh: 对于那些能让你觉得“好的，这个候选人太棒了”的回答，以及那些让你觉得“嗯，可能不太行”的回答，你到底在寻找什么？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: There are some obvious check marks that are they able to first abstract out and figure out what the overall goals for the product are, who the users for that product are, what would they be focusing on right now, whether this will align with that or not. And then a reason backwards that okay, maybe this may not work, but something on these lines. Are you obsessed about this feature or are you obsessed about okay, what this enables you to do? So if this is what it enables you to do, then are you okay with considering some other options and so on? So I think that's the direction which usually goes in the right way.
turns.zh: 有一些明显的判断标准。比如，他们能否首先抽象出产品整体目标、用户群体、当前关注点，以及这些是否与产品战略相契合。然后，反向推导可能存在的问题，比如“或许这个方案行不通，但我们可以尝试其他思路”。我认为这种思维方式通常能引领正确的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: So the reason why I've not watched a lot of drama or TV recently is because I've discovered these short video apps through Instagram and all of these apps, they dub Chinese TV serials into English or there will be subtitles in English and they are delivered in TikTok style two-minute videos. And it's a masterstroke in how the series are constructed. The first few episodes, which is like 10 episodes which is about 10 to 15 minutes, sets up the story in such a way that you have to unlock the next 10. (01:06:47): And these videos are quite expensive. They end up, one series takes more than the entire cost of monthly cost of Netflix to view. But it's just amazing how the whole product has been put, how all these products have been put together on unlocking the lamification aspects of it, the storytelling aspects of it, the content cutting part of it, and even the selection of the stories part of it. And what I'm told is that once I've learned about it, I've also been reading about it, they're actually companies which are able to give you tools of where you can construct this app yourself. And multiple people, two-people, three-people companies are churning these out and earning a lot of profit from it as well.
turns.zh: 我最近不怎么看电视剧和电视节目了，因为通过Instagram发现了这些短视频应用。这些应用会把中国电视剧配音成英文，或者加上英文字幕，还以TikTok式的两分钟视频形式呈现。整个剧集的结构设计堪称神来之笔。前几集（通常10集，每集10到15分钟）会铺垫故事背景，让你迫不及待想解锁后续内容。（01:06:47）这些视频价格不菲，一部剧集的观看费用可能超过Netflix一个月的订阅费。但整个产品生态的打造令人惊叹——从解锁机制、叙事设计、内容剪辑到故事选材，无不精心打磨。据说了解这些后，你还能找到相关工具自己开发这类应用。现在有很多二人团队、三人团队在开发这类产品，并从中赚取丰厚利润。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is this called for people that want to check this out?
turns.zh: 对想了解这些的人来说，应该怎么操作？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: So you can start with DramaBox, you can start with [inaudible 01:07:47] Reels and so on. And there are multiple of these. And those of you who are very familiar with TikTok, you would've seen that some of these show you the first 10 episodes on TikTok and then they take you to their app to view the rest.
turns.zh: 可以从DramaBox开始，或者[未听清 01:07:47] Reels等平台。类似产品还有很多。熟悉TikTok的用户可能注意到，有些平台会在TikTok上播放前10集，再引导用户到应用内观看后续内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I love so many unusual contrarian pieces of advice here, I love it. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to, share with friends or family, either in work or in life?
turns.zh: 哇哦。我超爱这里这么多与众不同的逆向建议，太棒了！还有两个问题：你有没有一条自己常挂在嘴边的人生格言，无论是在工作还是生活中，都会反复提及、与朋友或家人分享？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: For me, the most important thing has been that I started my career very late in tech. I was already 25. For the first several years, I worked in a small [inaudible 01:08:32] town in India. I came to Delhi only in 2013, and I joined Gojek in 2018. I think I've done reasonably well for myself. And it's never late to do or what do you want to do and what do you want to be. I think that's the thing that I really, really believe in and I also advise in. Especially as the world is aging and a lot of people are thinking about it, I would say that it's not too late ever. You can be and do what you want right now.
turns.zh: 对我来说，最重要的是我在科技行业起步很晚。当时我已经25岁了。最初的几年，我在印度的一个小镇工作（这里有音频缺失）。2013年我才来到德里，2018年加入了Gojek。我觉得自己做得还不错。无论是想做什么、想成为什么样的人，都不算晚。我真的非常相信这一点，也经常给别人这样的建议。尤其是当世界人口老龄化，很多人都在思考这个问题时，我想说永远都不算晚。你现在就可以成为并做你想成为的人，做你想做的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So good. It's not too late. I really, really like that advice. My wife is an illustrator designer. She has a book she put out called Am I Overthinking This? It's in my background somewhere there. And she has a chart that communicates that exact message in a really cute way, and we'll try to link to it in the show notes. Final question. You live in Singapore, I know you travel a lot. But if someone were to come to Singapore, is there a food that you think they need to try that's unique to Singapore?
turns.zh: 太棒了。永远都不算晚。我真的很喜欢这个建议。我妻子是一名插画设计师。她出版了一本书，叫《我是不是想太多了？》（Am I Overthinking This?），我记得在我的背景里有提到这本书。她设计了一张图表，用一种非常可爱的方式传达了这个观点，我们会尽量在节目笔记中附上链接。最后一个问题。你住在新加坡，我知道你经常旅行。但如果有人来新加坡，有没有什么独特的新加坡美食值得他们尝试？

turns.speaker: Vikrama Dhiman
turns.en: Singapore? There are multiple. So Singapore is a melting pot of different cultures. There are four official languages. And the only thing I will advise is depending on your taste buds, whatever you want to do, you should go and visit a Hawker Center. And it's an amazing experience in itself. And those of you who've seen Crazy Rich Asians, the first thing they do when they land in Singapore is go to the Hawker Center. So it's an experience of its kind. And if you are looking for a specific recommendation, go to Lau Pa Sat. If you are a fan of Indian, you'll get that. If you're a fan of Malay cuisine, you'll get that. If you're a fan of Singaporean Chinese, you'll get that. So you pick what works for you.
turns.zh: 新加坡？有很多选择。新加坡是个文化大熔炉，有四种官方语言。我唯一的建议是，根据你的口味偏好，你想尝试什么，就去霍克中心（Hawker Center）看看。这本身就是一种很棒的体验。看过《摘金奇缘》（Crazy Rich Asians）的人都知道，他们刚抵达新加坡的第一件事就是去霍克中心。所以这是一种独特的体验。如果你想具体推荐，可以去刘家庄（Lau Pa Sat）。如果你喜欢印度菜，那里能满足你。如果你喜欢马来菜，那里能满足你。如果你喜欢新加坡华人菜，那里也能满足你。所以你可以根据自己的喜好选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
